title: Our first positive finding did not survive our own harder test
body: Last week we found that the layered self-sustaining sets in a map of biochemistry were not reproduced when we shuffled the network at random. We then built a shuffle that keeps every reaction chemically balanced, which the first one did not. Those chemically legal shuffles reproduce the layers exactly: the real network's three nested sets and its depth of three sit right at the middle of what random balanced networks give. So the layering is not evidence about the chemistry of early metabolism, and we have retracted that reading of our own result.

title: QT45's error threshold cannot be pinned down from its measured singles and doubles
body: Our second method, which keeps the measured pair effects, overestimated the planted threshold in every test landscape with only higher-order epistasis (0 of 5 within 20%), while the first method underestimated it by about 27%. The two reasonable extrapolations bracket the truth from both sides, so we closed this line without computing a real threshold.

title: The LUCA estimate survives realistic gene-tree errors
body: On three simulations with a known first genome and gene trees inferred the way real studies do, the method recovered 0.96, 1.03 and 1.04 times the true number of genes (mean 1.01), inside our sealed 0.8 to 1.25 pass range. These simulations lean on the fitted weight far less than the real data do, so this does not validate the published 2,600 genes.

title: Bigger trees give the same LUCA estimate, but one large gene family failed
body: With 160 genomes per domain the method recovered 1.10 times the true number of genes. The reconciliation program failed on the largest gene family, a real LUCA family, so by our sealed rule the test is inconclusive; the 320-genome run was lost when the cloud machine was reclaimed.

title: The method could not tell a small LUCA from a big one when early genes moved between domains very often
body: In a preregistered simulation, a first genome ten times smaller, padded with gene families born just after the root that crossed between bacteria and archaea 4 to 7 times each, scored as large as the real-size one (2 seeds, loosely matched). This matters only if early exchange was about 100 times today's rate or more, which this does not show; without that exchange the small world could not be made to resemble the big one.

title: Next two LUCA tests written down before running
body: One checks whether the LUCA estimate holds as trees grow to more genomes; the other runs the hardest setting we could build. Both plans and their pass marks were fingerprinted before any run.

title: Right total, some wrong genes
body: In the same test, 10 to 18% of the probability the method placed on LUCA genes sat on genes that were not really there, and a similar share of real LUCA genes was missed, so the count comes out about right. The probabilities are only roughly calibrated: of genes given more than 0.8, between 88% and 97% were really in LUCA, and mid-range probabilities miss in both directions. So the right total comes partly from errors that cancel.

title: Yesterday's failed test was a laptop crash
body: The gene-tree program crashed on large gene families on the Mac, and every crash hid a real LUCA gene. On Linux the same simulation gives 1.09 instead of 0.75, inside the pass range, so the failed verdict no longer stands.

title: A sealed LUCA test failed its pass mark
body: On a simulation with a planted first genome, the method recovered 0.75 times the true number of genes at the largest setting, outside the 0.8 to 1.25 we set in advance. We traced it the next day (see above).

title: The size of LUCA rests on one fitted number
body: Moody et al.'s 2024 LUCA estimate depends almost entirely on one weight the method fits to the data: with the program's default setting the same data give about 34 gene families instead of about 1,290. The data strongly favour the fitted weight, so the question is whether that weight is accurate.

title: RNA contacts can't be read from this mutation data
body: We tried to read which parts of the self-copying RNA QT45 touch each other from 8,346 published double mutants. The method failed its own check on planted answers, and pairs added almost nothing once overall saturation was accounted for.

title: Scoring routes from published methods isn't repeatable yet
body: Two independent readers scoring the same prebiotic RNA routes from the papers agreed too little (kappa 0.22), so our sealed rule stopped the ledger.

title: Prebiotic papers report their methods as well as other chemistry
body: We expected origin-of-life papers to leave out more conditions than ordinary synthesis papers. Across 40 and 20 papers, none of the three predicted gaps appeared.
